**August 24, 1931 — a Monday**

You were born into a catastrophe. Not a sudden one — one grinding, and by August 1931, in its second year with no bottom yet in sight.

**The exact day — Britain's government collapses and rebuilds:** On August 24, 1931, Ramsay MacDonald's Labour government fell. The cabinet had fractured over whether to cut unemployment benefits — the bankers demanding austerity as the price of an emergency loan, the Labour Party's core refusing to savage the people it was built to protect. MacDonald went to the King, resigned, and then, in a move his own party experienced as betrayal, immediately agreed to lead a cross-party National Government. He was expelled from Labour the following week. The crisis consumed the government that existed when you were born and replaced it with a different one before the month was out.

**Twenty-eight days after your birth — Britain abandons the gold standard:** On September 21, 1931, Britain suspended the gold standard — the monetary framework that had governed international finance for a century. The pound would no longer be exchangeable for a fixed weight of gold. This was not a technical adjustment; it was an admission that the rules of the economic order could no longer be sustained. Fourteen countries followed Britain off gold within weeks. The world you were born into was operating on financial assumptions that collapsed before you were a month old.

**The Depression as the air you first breathed:** The statistics are familiar; the daily texture is harder to recover. In 1931, American banks were failing at a rate of several per week. Families who had considered themselves stable were discovering they weren't. Men who had held jobs throughout the 1920s were standing in breadlines. The Hoover administration, committed to the idea that markets self-corrected and that government intervention would only prolong the crisis, offered very little. Franklin Roosevelt — who would remake the relationship between citizen and government — was still governor of New York. The New Deal was 18 months away.

**The land itself was failing:** The Dust Bowl was beginning to form in the early 1930s, driven by drought and decades of over-farming the Great Plains. By mid-decade it would displace hundreds of thousands of families from Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and surrounding states — the people Steinbeck would later call the Okies. You were born as the ecological catastrophe that would become one of the defining images of the Depression was quietly taking shape.

**Fifty-five days after your birth — Thomas Edison:** Thomas Edison died on October 18, 1931, at 84. He had been alive for your entire life to that point. His inventions — the phonograph, the motion picture camera, the practical incandescent bulb, the electrical distribution system — were still the operating infrastructure of the world you were born into. A man whose formative years were the Civil War era was alive the day you arrived. You have now outlived him by 61 years.

**The medium of your childhood:** You were born into a radio world. Television was a laboratory curiosity in 1931; the first regular broadcasts wouldn't come until the late 1930s, and mass television was a postwar phenomenon. Radio was how families gathered for news and entertainment — how they heard Roosevelt's Fireside Chats, how they followed the war. You watched radio give way to television, television give way to the internet, the internet give way to something that still doesn't have a settled name. Each transition happened within your single lifetime.

**The war that defined your childhood, precisely:** You were 8 when Germany invaded Poland. You were 9 during Dunkirk and the Battle of Britain. You were 10 when Pearl Harbor brought the United States in. You were 12 when Stalingrad turned the war on the Eastern Front. You were 13 when Allied forces landed at Normandy. You were 14 when the atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the war ended. Most people who lived through World War II experienced it as adults. You experienced it as a child and adolescent — old enough to follow it, young enough to have it form the bedrock of your understanding of what human beings are capable of doing to one another.

**At 89 — the pandemic:** In 2020 and 2021, when you were 88 to 90 years old, COVID-19 moved through the world with particular ferocity toward the elderly. You survived it. The generation that had the most to lose from that pandemic — and that had already survived the Depression, the war, and nine decades of accumulated risk — lived through one more.

**At 95:** You were born 28 years after the Wright Brothers' first flight and have lived to see spacecraft land on Mars and a telescope photograph galaxies from 13 billion years ago. You were born when Herbert Hoover was president and have outlived every president since. You arrived in the worst year of the worst economic crisis of the modern era, in a world that was 17 months from Hitler's rise to power and 8 years from global war — and you are still here, which is its own extraordinary fact.

The Monday you were born, Britain's government was dissolving, the gold standard was 28 days from collapse, and Thomas Edison had 55 days left to live. The world that held all of that is so remote from the present that it requires an act of imagination to believe a single human life bridges both ends. Yours does.
